caucusNote: Dec. 1 is the reported date for the secret caucus ballot. A majority of those present and voting is required. If everyone votes, that is 28 of 55, or 29 of 56 if the Alaska seat goes to Mary Peltola and she participates.
methodology: Public support includes the candidates and the latest explicit endorsement we found. Earlier endorsements count under the original public-record method and are labeled separately when they have not been reaffirmed after Van Hollen entered. Calls for change without a named pick are separate. Research leans are tentative editorial judgments based on the cited evidence. The ballot is secret.

senators.name: Mary Peltola

evidence.text: Peltola widened her first-choice lead in the Nov. 12 ballot count. Alaska’s Senate race remains uncalled, with ranked-choice tabulation scheduled for Nov. 18 if needed.
Alaska’s Senate race is uncalled. Peltola is shown only as a possible member of the incoming caucus.
Her campaign did not say how she would vote when asked in March.

senators.analysis: Her participation depends on the result and caucus eligibility. No leadership choice was verified.

evidence.text: Kelly said he plans to support Schumer after the midterm victories.
NPR reported on Nov. 12 that Gallego publicly supports Schumer. He credits the incumbent for winning the majority.

senators.name: Adam Schiff

evidence.text: Schiff served as a DSCC vice chair in the midterm cycle. No public leadership choice was found.

senators.analysis: His campaign role is a relationship to watch. It is too indirect to assign a lean.

evidence.text: Padilla said he looked forward to the caucus discussion when asked about the leadership vote on Nov. 10.
No public position on this contest was found in the sources reviewed.
Bennet declined to commit and said the caucus would have time to debate.

senators.name: Chris Murphy

evidence.text: Murphy did not commit to replacing Schumer when asked earlier this year.
Reporting identifies Murphy and Van Hollen among senators pushing for a change in strategy.

senators.analysis: Murphy worked with Van Hollen in a group pressing Schumer for a more confrontational strategy. This is a working alliance, with no declared vote.

evidence.text: Blumenthal confirmed he would vote for Schumer after previously calling for new ideas and energy.
Coons said the caucus should have an open discussion about its future.

senators.name: Lisa Blunt Rochester

evidence.text: Blunt Rochester helped lead Senate Democratic campaign work. No public leadership choice was found.
She credited Schumer for recruiting strong candidates in Nov. 2 reporting. She did not name a choice.

senators.analysis: Her praise of Schumer is a small signal toward continuity. Her campaign role alone does not indicate a vote.

senators.name: Jon Ossoff

evidence.text: Before the election, a senior campaign staffer declined to say whether Ossoff would support Schumer.

senators.analysis: This is a campaign response. Ossoff’s own current preference is unverified.

senators.name: Raphael Warnock

evidence.text: Warnock called for change and said he was willing to hear the case for anyone who wants to lead.

senators.analysis: His remarks leave both candidates in play.

evidence.text: Schatz endorsed Schumer and said on Nov. 12 that he would vote for him in the caucus election.
The public statement is recorded in the Nov. 13 whip count.

senators.name: Mazie Hirono

evidence.text: Hirono cosponsored Medicare for All. No public choice in the leadership contest was found.

senators.analysis: Shared policy priorities are too broad to infer a private leadership vote.

senators.name: Josh Turek

evidence.text: Turek declined to affirm support for Schumer when asked during the campaign.

senators.analysis: The available reporting does not establish which candidate he prefers.

senators.name: Juliana Stratton

evidence.text: Stratton’s campaign reaffirmed her opposition to Schumer after the general election.

senators.analysis: Van Hollen is the declared alternative to a candidate she has explicitly ruled out. She has not publicly named her pick in the sources reviewed.

evidence.text: No public position on this contest was found in the sources reviewed.

senators.name: Adam Hamilton

evidence.text: Hamilton said after the election that he would not support Schumer for leader.
Hamilton discussed wanting a leader who would govern from closer to the center.

senators.analysis: Opposition to Schumer opens a path for Van Hollen, but Hamilton has expressed interest in a leader closer to the center.

senators.name: Ed Markey

evidence.text: Markey answered a leadership question by emphasizing discussions about a progressive agenda.
Reporting describes Markey and Van Hollen’s work with the same group.

senators.analysis: He has worked with Van Hollen to press leadership on strategy. His current public remarks focus on the agenda.

senators.name: Elizabeth Warren

evidence.text: Before the election, Warren deferred questions about leadership until after the midterms.
Reporting describes Warren’s role in pressing for a different Senate strategy.
In a Nov. 10 interview, Warren declined to discuss leadership.

senators.analysis: She worked with Van Hollen on changing the caucus’s strategy. That does not settle her choice of leader.

senators.name: Angela Alsobrooks

evidence.text: NPR listed Alsobrooks among Schumer’s public supporters on Nov. 12, based on her position before her Maryland colleague entered the race.
Recent coverage distinguishes this earlier endorsement from the current public count.

senators.analysis: Earlier public support for Schumer. Axios reported on Nov. 13 that it had not been publicly reaffirmed since Van Hollen entered the race.

evidence.text: Van Hollen announced his run on Nov. 12. The public tally includes him as a candidate.
King publicly endorsed Schumer on Nov. 12. He caucuses with Democrats.

senators.name: Troy Jackson

evidence.text: Jackson said he had told Schumer he would support someone else.
In a Nov. 13 interview, Jackson said he wanted to judge Van Hollen on his own merits.

senators.analysis: His opposition to Schumer puts him in play for Van Hollen. He explicitly said he would not back Van Hollen simply because he is the alternative.

evidence.text: El-Sayed endorsed Van Hollen in a Nov. 12 statement after previously backing him as a possible challenger.

senators.name: Elissa Slotkin

evidence.text: On Nov. 13, C-SPAN reported that Slotkin said she would not vote for Schumer and welcomed more candidates into the race.
Drop Site’s tally records the refusal. Axios still lists her without a named endorsement.
Slotkin called for a different plan from any contender seeking her support, and discussed leadership with Van Hollen.

senators.analysis: Slotkin explicitly ruled out Schumer. She remains open to other candidates, so there is no public commitment to Van Hollen.

senators.name: Amy Klobuchar

evidence.text: Klobuchar remains a senator ahead of her transition to the Minnesota governor’s office. No public leadership choice was found.

senators.analysis: Her eventual Senate replacement is separate from the December caucus snapshot.

evidence.text: Flanagan named Van Hollen as her choice in a Nov. 13 post.
Drop Site updated her entry to reflect the named endorsement.
The Nov. 13 named tally also reports Flanagan’s endorsement.
Colom said he wanted to know his options before committing.
AP called the Mississippi race for Colom.
Colom emphasized rural and Southern voices while withholding a choice.

senators.name: Roy Cooper

evidence.text: Cooper’s campaign withheld a leadership choice when asked in March. No later commitment was verified.

senators.analysis: Recruitment alone is too weak a signal to assign a lean.

senators.name: Chris Pappas

evidence.text: Pappas declined to commit when asked on Nov. 12.
Pappas called for new voices after the election.

senators.analysis: He previously called for a new generation of leadership. He has left his choice open.

evidence.text: No public position on this contest was found in the sources reviewed.
Kim said he had not yet had the chance to discuss the decision with the caucus.

senators.name: Cory Booker

evidence.text: Booker praised Schumer’s midterm work and said the caucus would discuss leadership.
Tracks both his August remarks and his post-election comments.

senators.analysis: His praise for Schumer and earlier talk of generational change point in different directions.

evidence.text: Before Van Hollen entered, Luján noted that no challenger was running. He did not commit to a candidate.

senators.name: Martin Heinrich

evidence.text: Heinrich declined to publicly commit to Schumer in post-election reporting.
Earlier reporting placed him in the group working with Van Hollen to change caucus strategy.

senators.analysis: Working with Van Hollen on caucus strategy is a weak signal. Heinrich has not made a public pledge in the sources reviewed.

evidence.text: Cortez Masto reaffirmed support after Van Hollen launched his campaign.
Rosen backed Schumer after Van Hollen entered the contest.
Schumer said on Nov. 12 he was seeking another term and claimed he had enough votes. The public tally includes him as a candidate.
NPR reported on Nov. 12 that Gillibrand publicly supports Schumer. She chairs the Senate Democratic campaign committee.
AP’s Nov. 13 reporting confirms Brown is supporting Schumer.
Brown said he would support Schumer after winning Ohio’s special election.

senators.name: Ron Wyden

evidence.text: At a Nov. 9 press conference, Wyden declined to comment on Senate leadership changes.
Wyden described the party’s improved Senate prospects in an October interview.

senators.analysis: Wyden previously gave Schumer credit for Democratic prospects. His latest refusal to comment leaves the direction uncertain.

evidence.text: Fetterman told reporters on Nov. 11 that he would vote for Schumer, citing his recruitment of successful candidates.
Reed publicly endorsed Schumer on Nov. 12, citing his effectiveness in the job.
Whitehouse said after the election that winning the majority justified another term for Schumer.
Drop Site records his post-election statement as backing Schumer.

senators.name: Annie Andrews

evidence.text: Asked about Schumer, Andrews called for generational change in congressional leadership.

senators.analysis: Her call for change points toward a challenger in a two-person race. It does not name Van Hollen.

evidence.text: Talarico said he wanted to hear Schumer’s plans before taking a position.

senators.name: Mark Warner

evidence.text: Warner praised Schumer’s election work and declined to commit on Nov. 10.
Warner serves as a caucus vice chair in the current Congress.

senators.analysis: His positive assessment and current leadership role give a modest continuity signal.

senators.name: Tim Kaine

evidence.text: Kaine said in June that he would continue to support Schumer as leader.
The tracker records his Nov. 12 decision not to restate his earlier support.
Recent coverage distinguishes this earlier endorsement from the current public count.

senators.analysis: Earlier public support for Schumer. Axios reported on Nov. 13 that it had not been publicly reaffirmed since Van Hollen entered the race.

evidence.text: Sanders endorsed Van Hollen by name after the candidacy was announced.

senators.name: Peter Welch

evidence.text: Welch called for change regardless of who leads and said he wanted to see who entered the race.

senators.name: Maria Cantwell

evidence.text: Cantwell gave Schumer credit for the election result and said she would hear out the debate.
